scenario.name: F5 Security & Mandiant — F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Request Smuggling to Root RCE
scenario.shortSubtitle: F5 K000137353 / Praetorian · Apache-to-Tomcat AJP Smuggling, form_page Auth Bypass & tmsh RCE
scenario.overview: A front lobby receptionist counts sealed parcels differently from the back-office clerk receiving them on a conveyor belt. An outsider packs a second hidden work order inside one parcel so it bypasses the lobby badge desk, creates a new master clerk account, and runs unrestricted commands in the engine room. In this scenario (CVE-2023-46747, F5 Security & Mandiant, F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Request Smuggling to Root RCE), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: smuggling a Forged Second AJP Request Past, then using the Smuggled Admin Context to Create, then executing Arbitrary root Commands. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Smuggling a Forged Second AJP Request Past, then Using the Smuggled Admin Context to Create, then Executing Arbitrary root Commands, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates process, authentication, and network telemetry for CVE-2023-46747 across the documented kill chain.

stages.title: TMUI AJP REQUEST SMUGGLING (CVE-2023-46747)
stages.subtitle: Smuggling REMOTEROLE=0 & REMOTEUSER=admin over TCP 127.0.0.1:8009
stages.description: The outsider hands over a single oversized parcel at the lobby desk. The receptionist stamps the outer wrapper as harmless, while the back-office clerk splits the parcel along a hidden crease and treats the inner slip as a pre-approved manager order. The attacker sends an unauthenticated HTTPS POST request to a reachable TMUI endpoint (/tmui/Control/jspmap/tmui/locallb/workspace/tmshCmd.jsp). By carefully sizing the HTTP headers and body, mod_proxy_ajp on the front-end Apache server miscalculates the binary AJP packet boundary and forwards the attacker’s raw payload bytes as a brand-new, second AJP request (starting with the AJP magic bytes 0x12 0x34) to the back-end Tomcat server on port 8009, with the internal AJP header attribute SC_A_REMOTE_USER set to "admin" (spoofing a fully authenticated administrator session because Tomcat blindly trusts whichever username the front-end Apache proxy puts in SC_A_REMOTE_USER). In a two-tier Apache + Tomcat AJP architecture, Tomcat does not re-verify passwords; it assumes the front-end Apache server already checked the user’s login before setting SC_A_REMOTE_USER. Smuggling a raw second AJP frame inside the socket stream lets an unauthenticated attacker inject SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin directly into Tomcat. In the documented Suricata CVE-2023-46747 exchange from Threat Actor (AJP Smuggler) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT HTTP 200 (confirming that the AJP SMUGGLING POST request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 ROGUE ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATION VIA TMSHCMD.JSP). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ AJP SMUGGLING POST / ⇠#1 ALERT HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 Threat Actor (AJP Smuggler)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 F5 Syslog & Suricata SIEM).

stages.title: ROGUE ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATION VIA TMSHCMD.JSP
stages.subtitle: Executing tmsh create auth user via smuggled Tomcat request
stages.description: Acting under that smuggled manager stamp, the back-office clerk opens the staff roster book and writes in a brand-new senior supervisor badge with full building and workshop keys, even though nobody ever signed in at the front desk. Executing inside Tomcat under the forged REMOTE_USER=admin identity (which bypasses the outer Apache authentication filter entirely because the smuggled request was born behind the Apache gatekeeper inside the internal AJP pipe), the request invokes the internal TMUI UserCreate handler (/tmui/Control/form) to create a new local BIG-IP administrator account granted Administrator role and Advanced Shell (/bin/bash) terminal access. When Tomcat processes the smuggled /tmui/Control/form request with SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin, it communicates with the BIG-IP master control daemon (mcpd) to write the new administrator account into /config/bigip_user.conf. In the documented BIG-IP /var/log/audit exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd), BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd) responds with ACK Audit 01070417 (confirming that the CREATE AUTH USER request succeeded on BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 ROOT BASH EXECUTION & SSL PRIVATE KEY EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CREATE AUTH USER / ⇠#2 ACK Audit 01070417) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 F5 Syslog & Suricata SIEM).

stages.title: ROOT BASH EXECUTION & SSL PRIVATE KEY EXFILTRATION
stages.subtitle: Running arbitrary bash commands as root and dumping /config/ssl/ssl.key/
stages.description: Wearing the newly forged supervisor badge, the outsider walks directly to the engine-room command console and dispatches unrestricted maintenance directives across the entire traffic-routing building. Using the newly created admin account (or directly via a smuggled tmshCmd.jsp request), the attacker runs tmsh run /util bash -c "..." (abusing the Traffic Management Shell’s built-in "/util bash" utility to break out of the restricted appliance CLI into an unrestricted Linux root shell). With root access on the load balancer, they extract SSL/TLS private keys (/config/filestore/files_d/Common_d/certificate_key_d/, allowing them to decrypt HTTPS traffic for the company’s web apps) and backend server credentials. Because an F5 BIG-IP sits at the front of the datacenter terminating TLS connections and load-balancing internal servers, root access on the appliance exposes both private TLS keys and direct network paths into internal application VLANs. In the documented Auditd SYSCALL 59 exchange from BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd) to Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh, Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the TMSH BASH RCE request succeeded on Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh and completing the final execution objective of F5 Security & Mandiant, F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Request Smuggling to Root RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ TMSH BASH RCE / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ③ (#3 BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd)) to Node ④ (#4 Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 F5 Syslog & Suricata SIEM).
